topic: Speaking up: what to do when something at work doesn't feel right
scope_note: Generic across organisations. No single company's policy, no jurisdiction-specific legal advice, no statistics, no hotline numbers. Channel names vary by organisation.

facts.statement: People often stay silent about a workplace concern because they fear being wrong.
facts.caveat: Widely reported in research on workplace voice and silence; say 'often' or 'many people', never 'everyone'.
facts.reference_hint: Research on employee voice and silence, for example Morrison and Milliken (2000) on organisational silence

facts.statement: People also stay silent because they fear fallout, such as damaged relationships or retaliation.
facts.caveat: Fear of fallout is a common reported reason, not the only one, and not everyone who speaks up suffers it.
facts.reference_hint: Research on employee voice and silence, for example Morrison and Milliken (2000)

facts.statement: Another common reason for silence is the belief that the issue is not one's own business or that nothing will change.
facts.caveat: A common reported reason; present it as a belief people hold, not as a fact about the organisation.
facts.reference_hint: Research on employee voice and silence, for example Morrison and Milliken (2000)

facts.statement: Speak-up policies generally ask people to raise a concern in good faith, which means an honest and reasonable belief that something is wrong.
facts.reference_hint: Common wording of organisational speak-up and whistleblowing policies

facts.statement: A concern raised in good faith does not need proof, and the person raising it is not expected to investigate.
facts.reference_hint: Common principle of organisational speak-up policies

facts.statement: Good faith does not mean being right: a concern raised honestly that turns out to be mistaken is generally still treated as a good-faith concern.
facts.caveat: Typical of policies; knowingly false reports are different and are not covered. Details depend on the organisation.

facts.statement: A simple way to weigh a concern is to ask whether it might break a law, a policy or the code of conduct.
facts.caveat: A practical rule of thumb, not a legal test; if unsure, raising the doubt is still fine.

facts.statement: Another simple question when weighing a concern is whether it could harm someone, such as colleagues, customers or the organisation.
facts.caveat: A rule of thumb, not a legal test.

facts.statement: A third simple question is whether you would be comfortable if the action were made public.
facts.caveat: A common ethics heuristic sometimes called a publicity or newspaper test; a prompt for reflection, not proof of wrongdoing.

facts.statement: Typical speak-up channels are the line manager, another manager, HR, a compliance, legal or ethics office, and a confidential or anonymous speak-up line.
facts.caveat: Names and availability vary by organisation; the script should say 'check which channels your organisation offers'.

facts.statement: Raising a concern with the line manager is often the first and easiest route when the person is comfortable doing so.
facts.caveat: Many policies encourage this but do not require it; other channels are always an option.

facts.statement: When the line manager is involved in the concern, the person can use another channel, such as another manager, HR, compliance or a speak-up line.
facts.reference_hint: Common provision in organisational speak-up policies

facts.statement: Where an organisation offers an anonymous speak-up line, a person can raise a concern without giving their name.
facts.caveat: Only where the organisation offers it; anonymous reports can be harder to follow up because questions cannot be asked, so giving contact details when comfortable can help.

facts.statement: After a concern is raised, it is typically reviewed and, where warranted, investigated by people other than the person who raised it.
facts.caveat: Process and timing vary by organisation; the script must not promise an outcome or a timeline.

facts.statement: Organisations typically keep the identity of the person raising a concern confidential as far as possible.
facts.caveat: As far as possible, not guaranteed: an investigation or legal duty can sometimes make disclosure necessary.

facts.statement: Speak-up policies typically prohibit retaliation against people who raise a concern in good faith.
facts.caveat: Phrase it as what policies typically say. Legal protections differ by country, so do not state them as universal.
facts.reference_hint: Common provision in organisational speak-up and whistleblowing policies

facts.statement: If someone believes they are being retaliated against for speaking up, they can report that through the same channels.
facts.caveat: Typical of policies; the exact route depends on the organisation.

terms.definition: an honest and reasonable belief that something is wrong, whether or not it later proves true
a confidential or anonymous channel, where an organisation offers one, for raising concerns
punishing or treating someone worse because they raised a concern

not_claimed: You must have proof before you raise a concern.
You are expected to investigate before reporting.
Speaking up always ends someone's career, or never has any cost.
Every organisation has the same channels, names or timelines.
Legal whistleblower protection is the same in every country.
A confidential report can never be traced or disclosed in any circumstances.
Raising a concern guarantees a particular outcome or speed of action.
Any statistic on how many people stay silent or suffer retaliation.
